secondaryKeywords: what is a citation in local seo
metaTitle: Local Citations: What They Are and Which Matter
metaDescription: A local citation is any online mention of your name, address and phone. Here's which Indian directories are worth claiming and what NAP mismatches cost.
definition: A local citation is any online mention of your business name, address and phone number, whether or not it links to your website.
answer: A local citation is any online mention of your business name, address and phone number — a directory listing, a profile page, an association roster. Consistency is the point: when your details appear five different ways across JustDial, IndiaMART and your own footer, you split the signal you were trying to build.
takeaways: Two kinds: **structured** (directory listings with fields) and **unstructured** (a mention inside an article or a forum post). Both count; only the first is something you can go and fix.
Formatting differences in a phone number are the smallest version of this problem. Different numbers, an old address and a forgotten duplicate listing are the expensive version.
Ten to fifteen listings that Indian buyers actually use beat 500 submissions to directories with no readers.
Audit before you build. Most businesses already have citations they've forgotten, and half of them are wrong.

body: A **structured** citation is a listing on a site with fields for it: JustDial, IndiaMART, Practo, your Google Business Profile, Bing Places, an industry association's member directory. Name in one box, address in another, phone in a third. Machine-readable and easy to audit.

An **unstructured** citation is your business named inside ordinary content — a news article that mentions your clinic and the road it's on, a Reddit thread naming your restaurant, a blog listing five cafés in Indiranagar. No fields, no form, no way to edit it. These frequently carry more weight, because nobody self-submits them.

Both feed the prominence half of local ranking, and both help Google confirm that the business it has a record of and the business your website describes are the same organisation. Your [Google Business Profile](/glossary/google-business-profile) is the anchor all of them are being checked against.

sections.h2: NAP consistency, and the phone number question
body: NAP stands for name, address, phone. The citation industry has spent a decade telling Indian businesses that a difference in punctuation will sink their rankings. Here's the honest ranking of severity, worst first.
The five-format problem is real but mild. Modern matching normalises punctuation and country codes reasonably well — a landline written five ways is unlikely to be what's holding you back.

table.caption: The same Mumbai landline, written five ways across five listings.
head: Where it appears
How it's written

bullets: **Worst: a different number entirely.** A call-tracking number on one listing and the real line on another gives Google two businesses to reconcile, and gives customers a dead ring.
**Bad: an old address.** You moved in 2023 and eleven directories still hold the 2019 address. That's a genuine conflict about where you are, which is a distance signal.
**Bad: a duplicate listing.** Two profiles for one business split reviews, split links and compete with each other. Report duplicates rather than editing both.

**Bad: a name that isn't your name.** "Sharma Dental Clinic — Best Implants Bangalore" is keyword stuffing in a business name field, it violates Google's guidelines, and any competitor can report it in about forty seconds.
**Mild: formatting.** Fix it when you're in there anyway. Don't buy a package to solve it.

sections.h2: The Indian directories actually worth claiming
body: The list that matters is short, and it's mostly determined by where your buyers already look rather than by anything Google publishes. A restaurant's most valuable listing isn't a directory at all — it's Zomato, because that's where the decision happens.

table.caption: Where an Indian business should actually be listed, by type.

rows: Google Business Profile, Bing Places, Apple Business Connect, JustDial, your own contact page
Practo, Google, plus the hospital or chain profile if you consult there

Google, Sulekha, subject-specific portals your students already compare on

bullets: Add your industry body, your chamber of commerce, and any supplier or partner site that publishes a dealer locator. These are unglamorous, permanent and hard for competitors to copy.
Skip anything whose homepage is a submission form. If the site exists to collect listings rather than to serve readers, the listing is worth what you'd expect.

sections.h2: Auditing what's out there, and why bulk packages underperform
body: Before building anything, find what already exists. Almost every business over three years old has listings created by a former agency, an intern, a franchise partner or the owner's cousin — and nobody remembers the logins.
numbered: Search your exact business name in quotes. Then search your phone number on its own. Then search your **old** address. That third search is where the surprises live.
List every result in a sheet with the URL, the details shown, and whether you can claim it.
Claim and correct the top ten to fifteen. Report duplicates on Google rather than editing both copies.
Fix your own site first — footer, contact page and schema should all state one version of the truth, because that's the source everything else gets checked against.
Re-run the same three searches every six months. Listings drift back, particularly on aggregator sites that repopulate from old data.

callout.title: Why the ₹3,000 citation package underperforms
callout.body: It creates new listings on sites with no users, often with a slightly different business name than the one you already use, which adds conflicts rather than resolving them. And it can't do the two things that would actually help: claim the listings you've lost access to, and remove the duplicate holding your old address. That work is manual, it's dull, and it's the part being skipped. See what honest [local SEO](/services/local-seo-services) covers and what [it costs](/cost/local-seo-cost).

faqs.q: Do local citations still matter for SEO?
faqs.a: They matter less than they did a decade ago and more than sceptics claim. Their main job now is corroboration — confirming your business is real, is where you say it is, and does what you say it does. Consistent details across a dozen used directories is the goal, not volume.

faqs.q: How many citations does a local business need?
faqs.a: Ten to fifteen that people actually use, plus any industry-specific one your buyers compare on. After that the returns flatten hard. A dentist listed properly on Google and Practo is in better shape than one listed badly on 400 general directories.

faqs.q: Does inconsistent NAP formatting really hurt rankings?
faqs.a: Formatting differences — spaces, dashes, country codes — are handled reasonably well by modern matching. Genuinely conflicting information does hurt: a different phone number, a stale address, a duplicate listing, or a business name padded with keywords. Fix those first and worry about punctuation last.

Claiming and correcting your free JustDial listing is worth doing for anyone. Their paid lead packages are an advertising decision, not an SEO one — judge them on cost per qualified enquiry against your other channels, and don't let anyone tell you the paid tier improves your Google ranking.

faqs.q: What do I do about a duplicate listing I can't access?
faqs.a: On Google, use the "Suggest an edit" and duplicate reporting flow rather than creating a third listing. On other directories, look for a claim link and verify by phone to the number listed — which is often why it's worth keeping the old number redirected while you clean up.

faqs.q: Do citations need to link to my website?
faqs.a: No. A citation counts as a mention of your name, address and phone whether or not it carries a link. A link is a bonus and on most directories it's nofollowed anyway. The value is corroboration and, on the good directories, actual customers.
